pages.text: Two wooden computer benches had been donated to the JHS ICT room. Now they swayed sideways whenever students sat down to type. Taller learners also complained of aching wrists and stiff necks after double periods. In the Career Technology workshop, Kwabena, Efua, and Asana put on safety goggles, closed shoes, and aprons, and inspected the loose joints with Mr Mensah-Bonsu. “There are two faults,” the teacher said. “First, this timber was used green, before seasoning. As it dried, it shrank and warped. Second, look at the frame. It is a plain rectangle with nothing across it. Push it sideways and it leans over into a parallelogram.”
sentences: Two wooden computer benches had been donated to the JHS ICT room.
Now they swayed sideways whenever students sat down to type.
Taller learners also complained of aching wrists and stiff necks after double periods.
In the Career Technology workshop, Kwabena, Efua, and Asana put on safety goggles, closed shoes, and aprons, and inspected the loose joints with Mr Mensah-Bonsu.
“There are two faults,” the teacher said.
“First, this timber was used green, before seasoning.
As it dried, it shrank and warped.
Second, look at the frame.
It is a plain rectangle with nothing across it.
Push it sideways and it leans over into a parallelogram.”
pages.alt: Inside a well-ordered JHS Career Technology workshop, students in goggles and aprons examine a leaning rectangular wooden bench frame that is tilting sideways under pressure.

pages.text: Mr Mensah-Bonsu pinned four cardboard strips into a rectangle. One push, and it folded flat. Then he pinned three strips into a triangle. However hard the students pushed, it kept its shape. “A triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides changes length,” he explained. “So we add a diagonal strut to a rectangular frame and turn it into two triangles. That is called triangulation. You will see it in roof trusses and bridges. And we use timber only after proper seasoning, so that it will not shrink later and split the joints.”

Then he pinned three strips into a triangle.
However hard the students pushed, it kept its shape.
“A triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides changes length,” he explained.
“So we add a diagonal strut to a rectangular frame and turn it into two triangles.
That is called triangulation.
You will see it in roof trusses and bridges.
And we use timber only after proper seasoning, so that it will not shrink later and split the joints.”
pages.alt: Mr Mensah-Bonsu demonstrating a floppy four-strip cardboard rectangle collapsing beside a rigid three-strip triangle and a timber roof-truss model.

pages.text: Before anyone touched a saw, Efua made a scale drawing. Her scale was 1 : 10, so one centimetre on paper stood for ten centimetres of real timber. The space between the bench legs was a rectangle, 60 cm wide and 80 cm high. Kwabena needed the length of the diagonal strut. Efua opened her Mathematics jotter. “The strut is the longest side of a right-angled triangle, so we use Pythagoras’ theorem,” she said. “c² = a² + b² = 60² + 80² = 3,600 + 6,400 = 10,000. The square root of 10,000 is 100. The strut is 100 cm long.” On her drawing, she ruled it exactly 10 cm.

pages.text: Meanwhile, Asana studied the health and safety notes from Computing. “Bad posture at a computer can lead to backache, eye strain, and Repetitive Strain Injury, or RSI,” she reported. “Fitting the workplace to the body is called ergonomics.” She measured volunteer classmates at a desk and listed the rules. Feet flat on the floor. Knees and elbows bent at about 90 degrees. Wrists straight, not bent up against the desk edge. The top of the monitor at eye level or slightly below, about an arm’s length away. And the screen turned away from window glare.

pages.text: Now came the workshop rule: measure twice, cut once. Kwabena measured the strut along a length of seasoned timber with a steel rule. He checked the right angles with a try-square and marked the ends to fit the joints. He clamped the wood firmly in the bench vice, kept his fingers clear of the blade, and sawed on the waste side of the line. The group fixed each strut with wood glue and screws. Efua then worked out the area of the tabletop, 1.5 m × 0.6 m = 0.9 m², so that they could buy enough varnish and waste none.

pages.alt: Kwabena in safety goggles clamping seasoned timber securely in a bench vice, checking a 90-degree corner with a steel try-square before sawing cleanly.

pages.text: Asana used Desktop Publishing software to design a poster, “Healthy Posture and Good Workshop Craft”, and hung it beside the repaired benches. On Monday morning, three students sat down together. Thanks to triangulation, nothing swayed. New monitor stands lifted every screen to a comfortable height. The benches were braced, sanded smooth, and varnished. Geometry, good materials, and ergonomics had done the job together.

activities.question: Why do carpenters add a diagonal brace (triangulation) to a rectangular frame?
options: Adding diagonal braces removes all gravitational weight from a desk
Triangles make green unseasoned timber dry out instantly without shrinking
A triangle cannot change shape unless a side changes length, stopping sway

activities.question: A rectangular frame is 90 cm wide by 120 cm high. Using Pythagoras’ theorem (a² + b² = c²), how long is its diagonal brace?
Which workstation setup follows good ergonomics and helps prevent RSI and back strain?
options: Monitor placed high with bright sunlight shining directly off screen
Elbows/knees at 90°, feet flat, wrists straight, screen at eye level
Sitting hunched with wrists bent sharply against a sharp table edge

activities.prompt: Put the design-and-make steps in the correct workshop order.
items: Investigate structural problem and select seasoned timber.
Draw 1 : 10 scale plan and calculate diagonal brace using Pythagoras.
Measure with steel rule, check 90° with try-square, and clamp in vice.
Cut, assemble triangulated joints, and apply protective varnish.

glossary.definition: Strengthening a frame by dividing it into rigid triangles using diagonal struts.
Controlled drying of timber to reduce moisture and prevent warping or splitting.
A structural piece designed to resist pressure in the direction of its length.
An L-shaped measuring tool used in woodwork to test and mark accurate 90° right angles.
